title: How Military Snipers Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how military snipers work, drawing on a HowStuffWorks article and an interview with an anonymous former Army Ranger sniper. Topics include the sniper team roles (sniper and spotter), reconnaissance and targets of opportunity, psychological and morale effects, overwatch and blocking positions, match-grade bolt-action rifles, scopes and ballistic compensation, the vapor trail of supersonic bullets, Gillie suits and their Scottish origins, Marine Corps Scout Sniper School training (Kim's game, stalking drills, observation games), and ballistic factors like gravity, wind, and minute of angle. The episode ends with a listener mail letter about living with MS and a happy outlook.

segments.title: Sniper team banter and cigarette superstition
segments.summary: The hosts joke about being a sniping team, with Josh as spotter. They discuss the superstition about lighting three cigarettes off one match, said to date from World War One trenches, and mention sniper video games.

segments.title: Sniper roles: reconnaissance, targets of opportunity, and psychological impact
segments.summary: Snipers do reconnaissance and observation as much as shooting, and take targets of opportunity such as officers, communications men, or material targets like generators. Their unseen kills hurt morale, making them force multipliers.

segments.title: Overwatch and blocking positions
segments.summary: The hosts describe the overwatch position in an elevated spot like a bell tower with a wide view of the battlefield, and the blocking action where snipers help defend a position from a roof. They note the film depiction in Inglorious Basterds and Saving Private Ryan.
topics: sniper positions in World War Two

segments.title: Sniper myth and team operation
segments.summary: The hosts say the lone gunman idea is not true, referencing the movie Shooter. Sniper rifles are crew-served weapons because two people are needed to shoot accurately, with the sniper in charge and the spotter in training.

segments.title: Mission planning, setup, and spotting
segments.summary: The team plans drop-off points, often a day's walk from the objective, chooses set-up positions, camouflage, escape routes and fallback positions. Once in place they may wait days prone while the spotter uses a powerful spotter scope to read wind, distance, and weather.

segments.title: Shooting, vapor trails, and correcting misses
segments.summary: The spotter confirms hits and calls corrections after misses. Supersonic bullets from large-caliber rifles create a visible distorted vapor trail. Spotters carry assault rifles for close combat because sniper rifles are poor at close range.

segments.title: Match grade rifles, bolt action, and scopes
segments.summary: Sniper rifles are often match-grade M14s or bolt-action rifles with free-floating barrels, fiberglass stocks, and handmade ammunition. Bolt action is preferred for accuracy, though semi-automatics are sometimes used. Scopes have about ten-power magnification with reticles. Rifles cost between eight and fifteen thousand dollars.

segments.title: Ballistics: gravity, wind, minute of angle, and sound
segments.summary: Snipers aim over targets because of gravity and adjust with a ballistic drop compensator for drop, wind, and temperature. Minute of angle is about 1.047 inches per hundred yards. Bullets go subsonic around 600 yards so distant targets may not hear the shot.

segments.title: Gillie suits and Scottish gillies
segments.summary: The Gillie suit is camouflage netting and padding worn by snipers. The name comes from Scottish gillies, game wardens who had to catch deer alive for mock hunts for landowners.

segments.title: Marine Corps Scout Sniper School training
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Marine Corps Scout Sniper School as highly selective, the Marines' sniper origins from 18th-century leathernecks, and training games including Kim's game (based on Kipling's Kim), stalking drills, and hidden-object observation exercises. Charles Whitman and Lee Harvey Oswald come up as non-military-sniper examples.
